title: Can England’s schools deliver the new reforms?
label: 15 September 2026 · Schools White Paper
summary: MPs questioned councils, academy-trust leaders and education experts about a wide-ranging plan to change schools in England. Witnesses broadly supported better help for children with special educational needs, stronger practical qualifications, more activities and closer ties with communities. But they warned that schools face too many simultaneous demands without enough money, staff or local flexibility. They disagreed over the benefits and accountability of academy trusts, and over how school performance and behaviour should be judged. Across both panels, a repeated message was that reforms must make schools more welcoming and give practical support to disadvantaged children rather than just add more targets.

chapters.title: Managing change and preparing for work
chapters.takeaway: Schools need time and money to carry out reforms, while technical education must lead to genuine opportunities.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Schools are being asked to do a great deal at once, from curriculum changes to helping pupils feel they belong. How can the Government make this manageable?

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: The White Paper sets out 102 separate policy commitments. Schools need a clear order for introducing them, a proper plan and funding. The changes to support children with special educational needs are particularly important, though doing nothing carries risks too.

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: Councils can help schools provide activities through libraries, leisure services and holiday programmes. But schools and councils know their communities best, so they need freedom over timing. Smaller and rural schools need particular help because they cannot spread costs across many schools.

turns.speaker: Caroline Voaden
turns.text: What about the new technical qualifications for teenagers? Can schools provide them, especially in rural places with few colleges, employers or specialist teachers?

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: Schools may have to change how they teach, but it is possible. The bigger question is whether young people will find jobs when they finish. Rural areas face additional difficulties arranging work placements and finding employers to work with.

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: Qualifications in practical and job-related subjects at age 16 currently lack the consistent national standards and oversight of GCSEs. The Government could bring forward its review of them by a year. Local councils and employers must also make sure there are good jobs and training opportunities afterward.

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: We must not make children choose at 14 and then trap them in that choice, especially where local options are limited. A broad education until at least 16 lets them combine subjects and change direction later.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The Government also wants more decisions made locally and two weeks of work experience for every pupil. What practical problems do you see?

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: I welcome more local responsibility, but what happens in places without an elected regional mayor? They must not lose out on funding. Councils need to work with schools and employers from childhood through to work. Two weeks of work experience is ambitious, but rural placements, staffing and money are real obstacles.

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: Academy trusts should work with councils and other local organisations to solve problems affecting children. Even large trusts operating nationally usually have local arrangements, so their size need not prevent that cooperation.

chapters.title: Academy trusts and parents
chapters.takeaway: Trusts say they can improve schools, but committee members challenge whether parents can hold them to account.

turns.speaker: Jess Asato
turns.text: The Government wants all schools to join or form academy trusts. Is there convincing evidence that trusts improve schools, given concerns about teachers leaving and weak local accountability?

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: Our recent research found substantial, lasting improvement after schools joined trusts, particularly schools in disadvantaged places. But results vary, and we cannot yet prove that joining the trust caused the improvement. Teacher retention figures are also disputed because the data do not distinguish clearly between leaving a school and moving within the same trust.

turns.speaker: Jess Asato
turns.text: Parents tell me that once they have raised an issue with the headteacher, they cannot find anyone further up who will answer them. Some trusts do not take part in local discussions. How is that accountable to communities?

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: Trusts must publish their accounts and details of their governing bodies, and they face yearly independent financial audits. I accept that large trusts can feel distant. Local governing arrangements matter because parents need someone nearby to speak to.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Please do not describe this as parents misunderstanding the system. Parents across the country have real difficulties getting answers when something goes wrong.

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: I was not blaming parents. I meant that the rules governing trusts are sometimes misunderstood. Complaints from parents have risen across all kinds of schools, not only academies. We all need to understand why parents feel disconnected.

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: I hear similar complaints. Some trusts need to do more to involve parents, although council-maintained schools are not perfect either. Having Ofsted inspect whole trusts, rather than just individual schools, might make their decisions more visible.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: The White Paper would allow councils to form their own trusts. Should they? And what about families who depend on schools for help with problems such as transport?

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: Some councils might want to set up trusts, but taking responsibility for tiny rural schools could be financially risky. It should be a choice, not a requirement. The White Paper also says too little about transport to school, especially the enormous cost of transport for children with special educational needs.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: To clarify, the proposal is to give councils the option to form trusts. It does not require them to do so.

chapters.title: School places and local powers
chapters.takeaway: Councils and trusts need to plan together, but cooperation alone may not be enough when schools refuse places or pupil numbers fall.

turns.speaker: Darren Paffey
turns.text: What should change when a child needs a school place, including partway through the school year? And how should we respond to falling pupil numbers?

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: The priority is to avoid children waiting a long time for a place. New legislation gives the independent official who settles admissions disputes more powers, but we still need to see the detailed rules. Schools and councils should try to agree first.

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: Councils can offer extra money when a school genuinely needs room for more pupils. But where a school can take a child and refuses, councils need stronger powers to secure the place. Admission limits should also be considered for children joining in later years, not just when they first start.

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: Falling birth rates are leaving some schools very small; one Lincolnshire school has just 21 pupils. We can share staff or leadership between schools, or put special-needs, alternative or early-years teaching on school sites. Closure should be the last resort.

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: Councils have the information on births and population changes, so they should bring schools and trusts together to decide how many places an area needs.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: But cooperation does not always happen. I have seen schools join trusts to escape local plans for reducing surplus places. Some leave debts with the council. Schools and trusts can pursue their own interests instead of what the whole area needs.

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: I agree. Councils need powers they can use as a last resort, whether a school belongs to a trust or not, to make sure there are enough places and appropriate support for children with special educational needs.

turns.speaker: Jodie Gosling
turns.text: You previously criticised RISE, the Government programme that arranges extra help for struggling schools. Has it improved?

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: Yes. At first, schools were not always matched with suitable organisations to help them improve. Those matches are now made more carefully, and many of the early problems have been resolved.

chapters.title: Activities, curriculum and money
chapters.takeaway: Extra opportunities can make school better for children, but witnesses resist one national model without the money to deliver it.

turns.speaker: Caroline Voaden
turns.text: How can children everywhere, including poorer pupils and those in rural areas, get activities such as music, sport and trips that go beyond ordinary lessons?

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: Councils can offer libraries, leisure centres and the HAF programme, which provides holiday activities and food for eligible children. I have seen how valuable that is, but in Lincolnshire we are reaching only some of the children who could benefit. More funding would help.

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: These activities help children discover talents, enjoy school and feel they belong. But schools are already under financial pressure. We must not make so many demands that we leave schools unable to provide them.

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: A longer school day might help some families. A trust in Bedfordshire has extended its day so children can do homework before going home to working parents. But that responds to local families; I would not impose the same timetable on every school.

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: A longer day also affects school buses and after-school care. The Local Government Association has not taken an official position on it.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Should the Government say more clearly which activities schools must provide and which should be offered outside school?

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: I would rather communities decided that. Government should set broad aims and provide the money. Special schools, for example, have particular difficulties arranging transport for activities.

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: Community organisations and youth centres can help too, but a centre that is easy to reach in a city may not be accessible in a rural area without transport.

turns.speaker: Peter Swallow
turns.text: What about Progress 8, the measure used to compare secondary schools’ exam results? Should it change to encourage a wider range of subjects?

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: We should keep it. English, maths and science are important, but pupils also need a broad choice of subjects. Adding a subject to the measure means removing another, which changes what schools prioritise. I want to see the Government’s actual proposals before deciding.

turns.speaker: Peter Swallow
turns.text: Should funding for disadvantaged children be more flexible, or would that take money away from the children who need it most?

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: Funding for disadvantaged pupils must be protected, but schools need some freedom to use it where children need help. I am not claiming that this is the Local Government Association’s settled position on the national funding formula; I will confirm that in writing.

chapters.title: Belonging, attendance and behaviour
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses argue that children attend and behave better when schools understand their needs, though targets and strict rules can create problems.

turns.speaker: Mrs Brackenridge
turns.text: Who should be responsible for improving attendance? And should parents be fined when children miss school?

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: Schools, councils and families all have a part to play. If schools can meet children’s special educational needs, that may help them attend. Before issuing fines, we need to know whether the reason is an avoidable holiday or a family in serious difficulty. A fine might make the latter worse.

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: England now collects daily attendance figures, which helps schools spot patterns. We have no settled position on fines, and evidence has questioned whether they work. They should be a last resort.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How important is a sense of belonging in the Government’s plans for schools?

turns.speaker: Dr Thompson
turns.text: It is central, not an optional extra. Research suggests children who feel welcome and understood are happier, achieve more and are more likely to attend. Schools should build trusted relationships every day, including with families, and recognise children’s needs before problems become serious.

turns.speaker: Dr Thompson
turns.text: England suspends and excludes proportionally more pupils than other parts of the UK. We focus heavily on behaviour rules, but we should also ask why a child is struggling. That means helping children build good relationships with adults and one another.

turns.speaker: Geoff Barton
turns.text: A good school has high expectations without treating children like soldiers. Teachers can explain things again when pupils struggle and teach them how to discuss, listen and disagree respectfully. That gives pupils more confidence to take part.

turns.speaker: Sam Henson
turns.text: The Government’s plan for improving engagement must not become another league table used to punish schools. Children themselves should have a say in what makes them feel part of their school.

turns.speaker: Mrs Brackenridge
turns.text: Attendance remains poor for many pupils. Would setting an individual attendance target for each school help?

turns.speaker: Geoff Barton
turns.text: Since covid, some families’ expectations about attendance have shifted. Schools need to rebuild trust with parents and explain why attending matters. I doubt that another system of targets will fix what is largely a relationship problem.

turns.speaker: Dr Thompson
turns.text: Some children are ill, afraid of school or feel they do not belong. Some parents are struggling, and some do not even know their child has missed lessons. Blaming or fining them will not solve those different problems. Support should come first.

turns.speaker: Sam Henson
turns.text: Targets can have unintended consequences. A school that works hard to improve attendance may still be judged poorly if the children it helps also have difficult behaviour. We should not reduce all these different circumstances to one number.

turns.speaker: Caroline Voaden
turns.text: Teachers also report serious problems with behaviour, sometimes enough to make them think of leaving. How do we keep classrooms calm without excluding children who need support?

turns.speaker: Geoff Barton
turns.text: Adults must demonstrate the respect and behaviour they expect, in lessons and around the school. Lessons that give children a voice and make subjects meaningful can also improve behaviour.

turns.speaker: Dr Thompson
turns.text: Teachers need more training to recognise trauma, emotional difficulties and unmet needs. Children cannot all behave identically, but staff can respond flexibly provided everyone remains safe and learning can continue. Training currently gives too little attention to this.

turns.speaker: Sam Henson
turns.text: Some strict rules, including on silence in corridors and uniforms, can create barriers and provoke conflicts that need not happen in the first place.

chapters.title: Exam results and useful skills
chapters.takeaway: International rankings provide only part of the picture; witnesses want stronger qualifications and better recognition of practical skills.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: What do the latest PISA international test results tell us about the direction schools should take?

turns.speaker: Dr Thompson
turns.text: PISA measures only part of education. Reading, maths and science matter, but league tables can push schools to chase rankings. We should also learn from schools where children feel safe, can speak openly and do well in their work.

turns.speaker: Geoff Barton
turns.text: People interpret those results to suit their arguments. Meanwhile, about a third of young people get below grade 4 in GCSE English. We should change how we recognise what these pupils can do, rather than leave them with a qualification that mainly tells them they have failed.

turns.speaker: Sam Henson
turns.text: The results have become a political argument, but they do not tell us what the pressure to achieve them has cost teachers and headteachers.

turns.speaker: Peter Swallow
turns.text: How can schools prepare young people for work and give practical subjects the same respect as academic ones?

turns.speaker: Dr Thompson
turns.text: We have promised equal respect for vocational qualifications before, but schools and employers often still treat them as second best. Good reading, writing, speaking and listening skills matter in every subject, including practical ones.

turns.speaker: Sam Henson
turns.text: We should ask pupils and parents what they need, rather than decide everything for them.

turns.speaker: Geoff Barton
turns.text: I sent some pupils to a nearby college for two days a week. They became more engaged, behaved better and did better in English and maths. The Government should focus on changes like that, the move to secondary school and pupils who miss out on a recognised English qualification, instead of adding so many requirements.

turns.speaker: Peter Swallow
turns.text: But with so many worthwhile additions, what should schools stop doing?

turns.speaker: Geoff Barton
turns.text: Reduce instructions from central government on how to manage attendance and behaviour. Trust teachers, improve teaching, give children meaningful choices and support pupils with special educational needs. We cannot do everything at once.

chapters.title: Making schools work together
chapters.takeaway: The final discussion questions whether compulsory trust membership helps, and calls for fairer support for disadvantaged children.

turns.speaker: Jodie Gosling
turns.text: Is moving every school into an academy trust really the right approach?

turns.speaker: Sam Henson
turns.text: First ask what a particular trust would do to improve a school. Some schools cannot find a trust that would help, while others regret joining one. We need better answers before insisting that everyone joins.

turns.speaker: Dr Thompson
turns.text: Some trusts provide excellent shared support, such as educational psychologists for children who need specialist help. Others do not. Some councils also do a good job, though many have lost resources. We should judge both by how well they support children, not by their name.

turns.speaker: Geoff Barton
turns.text: Competition can encourage schools to avoid children who need more support. One headteacher told me that a family had been steered away from another school because their child had anxiety. We need schools to share responsibility for every child, not shift difficult cases elsewhere.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What if a school wants to leave a distant trust and join one nearby, but its current trust refuses to release it?

turns.speaker: Sam Henson
turns.text: That is a real obstacle. Some trusts expanded to grow their numbers rather than because schools belonged together locally. I personally support making moves between trusts easier, but that is not yet the National Governance Association’s official position.

turns.speaker: Darren Paffey
turns.text: What would most help close the gap between disadvantaged children and their better-off peers?

turns.speaker: Geoff Barton
turns.text: We need good teachers and leaders to work and stay in the communities where they are needed most. But a poor Ofsted report can damage a headteacher’s career, making challenging schools less attractive. Leaders need support for improvements that take time.

turns.speaker: Dr Thompson
turns.text: Poverty exists in towns, cities and rural areas. Schools need extra help as soon as children’s needs become clear. Building a welcoming school culture can take years, so staff must not be punished while they are making meaningful changes.

turns.speaker: Sam Henson
turns.text: We should think more broadly about what disadvantage means, and encourage schools to take chances on pupils who need support. Local governors and community volunteers must have a real say in decisions or they may stop taking part.

turns.speaker: Geoff Barton
turns.text: Let school leaders choose the few changes that will do most for their pupils, especially the most disadvantaged, and then hold them responsible for the results. They cannot meet every new central instruction.

turns.speaker: Dr Thompson
turns.text: Give schools the time and support to change, and help them share scarce specialists, such as educational psychologists, across schools and councils.
